title: The river of being
hookLine: think how fast things pass by, like a river (Meditations 5.23)
last: WHAT AM I USING IT FOR.

lines: NOT ONE DROP IS THE SAME.
cards: A river has a name on the map. From a bridge it looks like one steady thing, the same river it was last year. But not one drop under the bridge now was there a minute ago.
The river is real, and it's also never the same twice. Centuries before Marcus Aurelius, a Greek thinker named Heraclitus made that observation well-known.
Marcus picked it up and turned it on everything, including himself.

teach.h: THINK OFTEN HOW FAST THINGS PASS.
teach.b: Think often, Marcus writes in book five, entry twenty-three, how fast the things that are, and the things coming to be, are carried past and out of sight. Not once: a habit of seeing.
Being itself, he says, is like a river in continual flow. Its activities keep changing, its causes shift in countless ways, and almost nothing stands still.
Heraclitus, as Plato reports him, said you could not step into the same river twice. Marcus lays that river over the whole world: cities, bodies, moods, reputations, problems.

And close beside us, he says, is the boundless gulf of past and future, into which everything vanishes. We met that gulf near the end of book four; here it's the sea the river runs into. Then the practical turn.

teach.h: WHY BE PUFFED UP OR TORMENTED?
teach.b: Isn't it foolish, he asks, to be puffed up, or tormented, or upset by these things, as if any of them would trouble us for long? A worry flooding in today is water, already moving. A flush of pride is water too.
The river picture works in both directions. It softens the hard thing, because it will pass. And it keeps the good thing light, so you enjoy it without clutching.
You don't have to stop the river. You only have to stop pretending it's a lake.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes watch moving water and recall Meditations 5.23, letting both worries and successes be seen as part of a constant flow.

o: the Greek thinker of the river you can't step in twice
a Greek hero well-known for his great strength and labors
a Roman poet who wrote about rivers and the open sea

p: no stepping in the same river twice
past and future, where all vanishes

s: Heraclitus, centuries before him, made it well-known, as Plato reports.
Marcus says to think about the flow often
think often, he writes, how fast things are carried past.
Marcus uses the river only for hard things

games.q: you get great news at work and feel on top of the world, sure this will last. what fits Meditations 5.23?
o: enjoy it, lightly, as water moving past.
build your whole identity on it.
refuse to enjoy it at all.
games.why: Marcus asks why anyone would be puffed up by what's carried past so quickly: enjoy it without clutching.

practice: Watch flowing water if you can, a stream, a fountain, a tap running slowly, or picture it, and watch it pass one point. Let one feeling you're carrying today, heavy or light, float into the water and move on. Breathe with the flow.

wordCard.voice: Heraclitus. The Greek thinker whose river said nothing stays the same, and whose picture of flow Marcus borrows for all of being. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'river': Marcus says being is like a river in continual flow.

carryVoice: Your line: the river. Worry or win, it's already moving. That's day five hundred sixty-nine.
